predecessors.name: Assyrian Egypt
predecessors.text: all of Egypt as the vassal kingdom of Psamtik I held it at independence (the Delta from 664, Upper Egypt from 656), drawn with the -615 shape

successors.name: Achaemenid Empire
successors.text: Egypt, conquered by Cambyses II in 525 ('First Achaemenid conquest of Egypt', 'First Egyptian Satrapy'); Cyprus had already passed to Persia in 545 (Ancient history of Cyprus page)

ledger.x: 655: Psamtik I of Sais throws off Assyrian overlordship and rules all Egypt as an independent king.
605: Egypt loses the Levant to Babylon at Carchemish.
Same year: the Phoenician cells of Cyprus (Kition's area) pass to Egypt in Cliopatria's shapes.
525 BC: the Saite Dynasty ends with the Persian conquest.

wars.name: Saite-Babylonian conflict over the Near East and Egypt
wars.outcome: Egypt was 'driven back' from the Near East by Nebuchadnezzar II; Apries 'held back Babylonian attempts to conquer Egypt'; the Babylonian invasion of about 568-567 'gained a foothold' but 'were repelled by Amasis' forces'.

wars.name: Necho II's Syrian war (Megiddo to Carchemish)
wars.outcome: Babylonian victory: Nebuchadnezzar 'led them to a decisive victory over the Egyptians at Carchemish in 605 BC' and 'conquered Egyptian territory from the Euphrates to the Brook of Egypt'; Necho 'was unable to recover any significant part of his lost…

wars.name: Psamtik II's Nubian campaign
wars.outcome: Heavy Egyptian victory, no gain: 'Psamtik II led a foray into Nubia in 592 BC'; the army 'advanced to Pnubs (Kerma) and the capital city of Napata in a series of fierce battles' and inflicted 'a heavy defeat ... upon the kingdom of Kush', then 'retreated back…

wars.name: First Achaemenid conquest of Egypt
wars.outcome: Persian victory: Psamtik III captured and later executed; Egypt became the First Egyptian Satrapy.

certainty.note: No treaty or survey line on the pages opened; the southern frontier is 'as far as the First Cataract' (a natural landmark, 'Elephantine continued to be the southern border of Egypt') and the Libyan, Sinai and Nubian edges are approximate.
